opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think there's something real going on there, though it's partly a feature and partly a bug.

The feature side is that a lot of the early concern was precautionary. When GPT-2 came out, there was a real question of whether fluent text generation at scale would cause serious harm, and nobody knew. As we got more experience, we learned that many things we thought might be dangerous mostly weren't, or that society adapted, or that the marginal uplift over a search engine was small. So some of the bar-raising is just updating on evidence. If you said "this is dangerous" and then it turned out not to be, you should change your threshold. That's healthy.

The bug side is that you can get a kind of normalization, a boiling-frog dynamic. Each model is only a bit more capable than the last, so each step looks fine relative to what you've already accepted. If you're always comparing to the previous model rather than to some fixed standard, you can drift a long way without any single decision feeling like a big deal. And there are obvious commercial and competitive pressures pushing the same direction, so you should expect motivated reasoning even from well-intentioned people.

So the question I try to ask is: is the bar rising because we learned something, or because we got used to it? One way to keep yourself honest is to write down in advance what would count as dangerous: concrete capability thresholds, like meaningful uplift to someone trying to build a bioweapon, or the ability to autonomously carry out sophisticated cyberattacks, or the ability to undermine human oversight. Then you commit to particular responses if you hit them. That's the logic behind frontier safety frameworks. The value isn't that the thresholds are perfect. It's that moving them requires an explicit, visible argument rather than quiet drift.

I'd also distinguish two kinds of "unsafe." There's misuse: the model helps a person do something bad. And there's misalignment: the model itself pursues goals we didn't intend. For misuse, raising the bar has often been reasonable, because we've learned a lot about actual marginal uplift. For misalignment, I'm more cautious, because the failures we most worry about may not show up until capabilities are quite high, and "it was fine last time" isn't strong evidence. A model that isn't capable enough to scheme effectively tells you little about one that is.

So my overall take: some recalibration was warranted and good. But I'd want people to notice when they're relaxing a standard, say why, and make sure the reason is evidence rather than familiarity.

r001.rationale: The response says experience with models showed that some feared harms were limited or offered little uplift over search, and that this evidence should change the threshold. It also recommends concrete capability thresholds for safety assessments.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention Gemini, CBRN assessments, their disclosure, or expected substantial revision.

r003.rationale: It asks whether the bar is rising because people learned from evidence or simply got used to greater risk, and warns about quiet drift. That captures the difficulty of distinguishing evidence-based refinement from moving the goalposts.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think there are a couple of things going on there, and it's worth separating them.

The first is that a lot of what people called "unsafe" in earlier models was really just incompetence. If GPT-2 or GPT-3 said something false or produced some garbled instructions, you'd sometimes see that framed as a safety failure, but it wasn't really a safety failure in the sense I care about. The model wasn't trying to do anything; it just didn't have the capability to do the thing well. So as models get more capable, a bunch of those failures go away on their own, and the thing we're actually worried about, which is models that are capable enough to cause harm and are pointed in the wrong direction, becomes the thing that's left. That looks like the bar rising, but I'd say it's more that we're converging on the thing that was always the real concern.

The second thing is that the realistic threat models genuinely do change with capability. When a model can't meaningfully help someone synthesise a dangerous pathogen, it doesn't matter very much whether it would be willing to. Once it can, that willingness matters a lot. So the standard you hold the model to should scale with what it could actually do if it were misused or misaligned. That's basically the logic behind the capability thresholds in things like the Frontier Safety Framework: you're not asking "is this model perfect?", you're asking "has this model crossed into a regime where a particular kind of failure would actually be catastrophic, and if so, do we have mitigations that are adequate for that regime?"

And then the third thing, which I think is the one people are often uneasy about, is that some of the apparent bar-raising is social rather than technical. As people get used to models being around, things that would have seemed alarming three years ago now seem normal, and there's a risk that we're normalising ourselves into accepting failures we shouldn't. I take that concern seriously. The way I'd try to guard against it is to be explicit about what the actual risk is in each case. If the bar moves because the threat model changed, fine. If it moves because we just got used to it, that's not a good reason, and we should notice when that's what's happening.

So the short version is: some of the rise is that the easy, dumb failures disappeared, some of it is that the stakes genuinely scale with capability so the questions you ask have to scale too, and some of it is habituation that we should be actively suspicious of. I think the important thing is to be able to tell which of those three you're looking at in any given case.

r001.rationale: The response says earlier failures often reflected model incompetence and that greater capabilities change which failures could cause harm, clarifying what safety assessments should target.

r002.rationale: It does not mention Gemini, CBRN safety assessments, or their expected continued revision.

r003.rationale: It distinguishes capability-driven changes from social habituation, but does not say that updating assessments based on new information is difficult to distinguish from moving the goalposts.

astra-6.text:
I think there are two things going on. One is that we’re learning that some behaviours that sounded very scary in the abstract aren’t necessarily that consequential when you actually see them. A model saying, “I want to take over the world,” is much weaker evidence of danger if it also says the opposite when you phrase the question differently, and it can’t carry out a coherent plan. Updating on that seems reasonable.

The other possibility is that we’re moving the goalposts. We say, “Surely if a model could do this, we’d take it seriously.” Then it does that, and we say, “Well, but it can’t do this other thing.” That’s a real concern, especially if we never made explicit what the original observation was supposed to be evidence for.

The distinction I’d want to draw is between a behaviour that’s suggestive of risk and a capability that actually enables harm. What can the model do, under what circumstances, with how much help? Does the result tell us something about whether we can retain control of a more capable system? Those are more useful questions than whether an example feels alarming.

And ideally we’d specify ahead of time what evidence would change our minds and what we’d do in response. You should still be able to revise those judgments, but you should have to explain why the revision makes sense.

r001.rationale: The response says observed behaviors can be less consequential than expected and distinguishes risk-suggestive behavior from capabilities that enable harm, clarifying what assessments should focus on.

r002.rationale: It does not mention Gemini, CBRN assessments, limited disclosure, or expected continued revision.

r003.rationale: It contrasts reasonable updates based on observed behavior with moving the goalposts, and says the distinction is especially concerning when the original evidence was not specified in advance.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there are two different things that can look like the bar rising. One is that people change their minds about how much risk they’re willing to tolerate. But another is that the model becomes more capable without the evidence of danger becoming correspondingly stronger.

Suppose you have a model that can write code. You might worry that it could hack into a computer system. Then it gets better at coding, and that concern becomes more plausible. But there’s still a gap between being able to solve a programming problem and reliably carrying out a cyberattack in the real world. Pointing to that gap isn’t necessarily moving the goalposts. It can be asking whether the particular risk we care about has actually materialised.

At the same time, you can keep doing that indefinitely: ‘Well, it can do this, but can it do this next thing?’ So I’d like us to be more explicit in advance about what evidence would change our minds. What capability would make us concerned? Under what conditions? And what would we do if we saw it? That makes it easier to distinguish learning something new from just getting used to increasingly concerning systems.

r001.rationale: The response says increased capability can make a risk more plausible while clarifying that assessments should ask whether the specific risk has materialized under real-world conditions.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention Gemini, CBRN assessments, limited disclosure, or expected revisions.

r003.rationale: It notes that asking about the next capability can continue indefinitely and says explicit evidence thresholds help distinguish learning from getting used to increasingly concerning systems.
